purpose: Machine-readable guardrail for hyperscaler, cloud-native, and Kubernetes-native lane work. This keeps active plans on controller reconciliation, Buck2/Prow evidence, trusted controller-owned required context, restricted workload security, generated shared surfaces, provenance-backed artifacts, quota/fairness controls, policy-as-code admission, progressive delivery, observability-first control loops, and shadow-only adapters while rejecting live-mutation shortcuts and retired bridge authorities.

official_sources.establishes: Cloud-native architectures favor loosely coupled, interoperable, observable, resilient services rather than shared mutable bottlenecks.
CUE can validate and export Kubernetes configuration, making it suitable as the first-party typed desired-state authority for cloud-cell manifests.
CUE is a constraint/unification language; Rust feature parity requires language-semantics conformance rather than template replacement.
CUE export materializes concrete data from evaluated configuration, so generated KRM parity must be tested before replacing CUE tooling.
CUE modules and imports are part of the compatibility surface for any Rust-native desired-state engine.
Helm charts package Kubernetes resources and are retained as external chart or temporary compatibility adapters, not first-party policy authority.
Kubernetes controllers reconcile observed state toward desired state through control loops.
Restricted Pod Security establishes least-privilege pod/container defaults for untrusted workloads.
NetworkPolicy supports pod traffic isolation and default-deny policy shape.
Kubernetes securityContext controls non-root execution, privilege escalation, read-only root filesystems, seccomp, and Linux capabilities.
RuntimeClass selects container runtime configuration for pod-level runtime isolation.
Pods can opt out of automatic ServiceAccount token mounting.
Draining evicts workloads through Kubernetes APIs instead of blind pod deletion.
ProwJob configuration is the compatible pattern input for presubmit, postsubmit, periodic, and batch CI jobs.
Prow's trigger-to-ProwJob-to-pod-to-status lifecycle is the compatible shape for disposable CI compute.
Prow pod utilities fetch source, wrap execution, and upload logs/artifacts outside the job pod.
Pods are ephemeral execution units; controllers recreate rather than depend on persistent pod identity.
Kubernetes local ephemeral storage must be requested/limited for bounded pod scratch I/O.
Buck2 remote execution uses remote action cache and CAS endpoints, matching content-addressed remote cache patterns.
GitHub Actions hardening recommends least-privilege token permissions, careful secret handling, and action supply-chain hygiene for the temporary bridge.
GitHub OIDC supports short-lived cloud credentials bound to workflow identity instead of long-lived static secrets.
SLSA v1.2 defines supply-chain levels and provenance expectations for source and build artifact integrity.
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy uses CEL rules to accept or reject Kubernetes objects without mutating them.
Kubernetes ResourceQuota constrains aggregate namespace resource consumption.
Kubernetes PriorityClass and preemption model priority/fairness tradeoffs for scheduled pods.
GitHub merge queue can use GitHub Actions or an external CI provider for required checks on queued merge groups.
Prow Tide manages a pool of GitHub PRs and batch ProwJobs against merge criteria.
OpenTelemetry models logs, metrics, traces, and events as observability signals.
Kubernetes Leases support lightweight coordination including leader election and node heartbeat-style coordination.
Kubernetes TTL-after-finished can automatically clean up completed Jobs after a bounded lifetime.
Topology spread constraints control how Pods distribute across topology domains for availability and blast-radius reduction.
PodDisruptionBudgets bound voluntary disruption for applications that need availability during maintenance.
API Priority and Fairness controls Kubernetes API-server request concurrency and queues by priority level.
Kubernetes RBAC grants permissions through Roles/ClusterRoles and bindings and should be scoped to the needed API access.
Kubernetes Secret handling requires encryption, least-privilege API/watch access, and careful workload isolation.
Taints and tolerations repel workloads from unsuitable nodes and support dedicated-node isolation.

required_patterns.implementation_hook: Prow/Kubernetes-native controllers own desired-state reconciliation; local specs are static evidence only.
Only the trusted oya-ci controller rollup may publish the durable oya-ci-required context.
Buck2 targets remain the build/test/check authority; Cargo/Tarpaulin/local scripts are advisory unless projected into Buck2/Prow evidence.
CI workloads use workload identity, block node metadata access, and reject static cloud secrets.
Generated controller config requires no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystems, non-root users, RuntimeDefault seccomp, and dropped ALL capabilities.
Default-deny network policy is required before explicit lane-owned egress/ingress grants.
Untrusted PR jobs run through a sandboxed RuntimeClass and restricted runner ServiceAccount.
Service-to-service traffic records mTLS intent and must later bind to mesh identity before production claims.
Shared files stay pointer-thin or generated from lane-owned shards to reduce merge conflicts.

First-party cloud-cell and pod desired state is authored as lane-owned CUE packages with generated Kubernetes manifests checked by buck2 build //:cloud-cell-elasticity-policy-check; Helm is adapter compatibility only.
Helm charts can be consumed for external ecosystems or emitted as temporary compatibility wrappers, but hand-authored Helm templates are not first-party policy authority.

A Rust-native CUE-compatible desired-state engine is a future native seam, not current authority until it proves restricted-subset parsing, CUE unification/constraint compatibility, module/import compatibility, deterministic generated-KRM parity, and golden output comparison against upstream CUE through Buck2/Prow.
Scale-to-zero requires workload-class eligibility, trigger source, idempotency, cold-start SLO, backpressure, rollback, and quota/fairness evidence before live use.
GitHub/GitHub Actions adapters remain temporary publication/shadow surfaces until native SCM/oya-ci/release conveyor cutover.
Pure-Rust-biased Sapling-inspired SCM owns change graph; oya-ci owns Buck2/Prow execution; release-conveyor-like CD owns progressive delivery ledger.
Cloud and Oyatie product auth/shared substrates stay decoupled now to avoid shared contract conflicts; later product rewrites consume Cloud IdP.

CI follows trigger -> fetch remote state -> compute/validate -> export artifacts -> destroy ephemeral workspace. ProwJob pods are disposable compute; SCM refs, CAS/cache, object artifacts, status, and audit ledger are durable.
Remote cache and CAS are allowed for performance but never correctness authority; cache keys are content-addressed and trust-domain separated.
Hot-path cache/artifact reads stay in the same region/cell as compute; cross-region replication is asynchronous and outside presubmit critical path.
Untrusted PR cache writes are quarantined; trusted postsubmit/periodic jobs promote warmed cache entries; scheduled cold-cache probes prove correctness without cache.
Job pods declare ephemeral-storage requests/limits and emit cache hit ratio, CAS bytes, artifact upload latency, and eviction metrics.
Builds run from pinned source/dependency/toolchain inputs and export immutable artifacts with SBOM/provenance/signature evidence before release-conveyor consumption.
Temporary GitHub bridge and native Prow jobs use short-lived OIDC/workload identity plus per-job least-privilege permissions instead of broad static secrets.
Admission policy rejects workload specs that violate restricted pod security, workload identity, network, quota, provenance, or controller-owned status invariants before scheduling.
Namespaces/cells declare ResourceQuota, ephemeral-storage budgets, concurrency limits, and PriorityClass policy so high parallelism cannot starve product or control-plane work.
Required Buck2 target inventory is computed from trusted SCM/controller state before candidate bytes are evaluated, preventing PR-authored changes from shrinking check scope.
Lanes edit disjoint shards; generated aggregates and Tide/merge-queue-style virtual merge heads validate combinations mechanically before fan-in.
Release-conveyor-style controllers gate canary, bake, promotion, and rollback on source-bound artifacts, SLO/error-budget signals, and audit ledger evidence.
Controllers and CI jobs emit structured metrics, traces, logs, events, and reconciliation decisions so status rollups are explainable rather than opaque green/red flags.
Highly available controllers use Kubernetes Lease-style coordination for leader election and heartbeat state instead of process-local locks or sticky runner identity.
Ephemeral Jobs and generated resources carry owner/cleanup metadata and TTL-after-finished policy so completed work is garbage-collected without manual sweeps.
Critical controllers, trusted jobs, and untrusted fanout lanes declare topology-spread, taint/toleration, and node-pool placement policy to preserve cell/zone blast walls.
Long-running services and controllers define PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful termination behavior before node drain or rollout automation is considered safe.
Native controllers, oya-ci, and SCM adapters classify Kubernetes API traffic through priority/fairness policy and bounded client concurrency.
Control loops use informer/watch/cache patterns with backoff and resync boundaries instead of unbounded list/poll loops against the API server.
Every controller and job has a lane-specific ServiceAccount plus minimal Role/ClusterRole grants; wildcard verbs/resources and shared cluster-admin identities are rejected.
Sensitive Kubernetes Secret material is KMS/envelope-encrypted, scoped by RBAC, rotated, and treated as a projection from a secrets authority rather than a durable app database.

forbidden_anti_patterns.rejects: Deleting pods directly as an operational plan instead of scaling, draining, pausing, or reconciling through controller-owned desired state.
A candidate PR, local script, or human-posted status acting as durable oya-ci-required truth.
Treating GitHub Actions as permanent first-class CI/CD authority instead of temporary compatibility/shadow evidence.
Jenkins, Forgejo, ArgoCD, Argo Workflows/Rollouts, or retired Oya CLI gates as active interim authority.
One shared hand-edited CI workflow as the coordination surface for parallel product/infra/cloud lanes.
New durable gate/check surfaces in Python or shell instead of Rust libraries, Buck2 targets, and Prow/Kubernetes jobs.
Reviving oya vcs, oya git, oya gate, or oya verify as sanctioned merge/CI authority.
Letting Cargo, Tarpaulin, or ad-hoc local tools outrank Buck2-native LLVM coverage and Buck2 check authority.
Treating hand-authored Helm templates as the first-party cloud-cell/pod configuration authority instead of CUE-owned constraints and generated Kubernetes manifests.
Allowing CI or service pods to reach node metadata APIs for cloud credentials.
Implicitly mounting default ServiceAccount tokens in CI/workload pods.
Privileged containers, privilege escalation, writable root filesystems, root execution, or retained Linux capabilities as defaults.
Running untrusted PR jobs without a sandboxed RuntimeClass.
Relying on open pod networking instead of default-deny plus explicit grants.
Long-lived CI runner pools with sticky workspaces, persistent checkout directories, or hidden runner-local state.
Treating pod-local disk cache, workspace contents, or a previous run's filesystem as correctness evidence or durable state.
Allowing untrusted PR jobs to populate the trusted cache namespace or share cache/write credentials across tenants, repos, or trust domains.
Placing remote cache/artifact hot-path reads across regions/cells, creating avoidable egress, latency, and correlated failure risk.
Overwriting logs, coverage, SBOM, or build artifacts in place instead of publishing immutable content-addressed artifacts.
Running CI pods without ephemeral-storage requests/limits, eviction metrics, or scratch-space budgets.
Privileged Docker-in-Docker or host socket mounts for untrusted jobs instead of sandboxed runtimes and controller-owned build/execution services.
Floating action refs, mutable image tags, or unpinned toolchain/dependency inputs such as @main, latest, or untracked local installs in authority-producing lanes.
Long-lived cloud keys, broad repository/org secrets, or PAT-style credentials exposed to CI jobs where OIDC/workload identity and scoped tokens should be used.
Letting a pull request decide which Buck2 targets, policy gates, or required contexts apply to itself without trusted baseline inventory.
Mixing trusted controllers, untrusted PR jobs, tenant workloads, and production control planes in the same namespace/cluster/account trust domain.
A CI pod directly mutating staging or production instead of handing signed artifacts/evidence to a release-conveyor/progressive-delivery controller.
Using kubectl apply/delete/patch from CI or local agents to bypass controller reconciliation, admission policy, review, or release ledger controls.
Using CRDs, ConfigMaps, annotations, or status fields as the primary application database for tenant/product domain state.
Running highly parallel lanes without quotas, concurrency budgets, PriorityClass policy, or cell-level fairness, creating noisy-neighbor and control-plane starvation risk.
Relying on one sticky runner, local file lock, shared shell lock, or process memory as controller leadership for oya-ci/SCM/CD control loops.
Leaving completed Jobs, generated objects, temporary namespaces, or workspace artifacts without owner/TTL cleanup metadata.
Letting trusted controllers, untrusted PR jobs, and critical services schedule anywhere without topology spread, taints/tolerations, or dedicated node-pool policy.
Force deleting pods or draining nodes for service/controller workloads without respecting PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful termination.
High-frequency list/poll loops, unbounded watches, or retry storms from CI/controllers that can starve Kubernetes API-server fairness queues.
Granting CI runners, Prow jobs, agents, or application controllers cluster-admin, system:masters, or wildcard verbs/resources instead of minimal roles.
Using Kubernetes Secrets as a long-lived product/application data store or broad shared credential bag instead of a scoped, encrypted, rotated secret projection.
Depending on humans or ad-hoc cleanup scripts as the primary lifecycle control for jobs, namespaces, workspaces, or generated controller resources.
